hints: Start with the breeding locations given - one in eastern North America and one in western North America. What would this mean for birds from the two areas meeting and breeding together?
If breeding between the two groups becomes rare or stops, think about what stops being exchanged between their gene pools.
Think about what happens independently in each separated group over 2.5 million years - new alleles arising and different environmental conditions in east versus west.
Link those independent changes to processes that shift allele frequencies and gradually make the populations genetically and phenotypically distinct.
walkthrough:
Separate by geography**
The original T. solitaria population became split into an eastern breeding group and a western breeding group. A physical distance or geographical barrier means individuals rarely meet. That is the start of allopatric divergence - populations in different places.

Cut off gene flow**
Because they breed in different areas, there is little or no interbreeding between east and west. So alleles are no longer shared by gene flow. Each gene pool is now isolated and will evolve independently.

Build up different genetic variation**
Random mutations occur separately in each population. The east and west also have different environmental conditions, such as climate, food, predators and habitat, so they exert different selection pressures. Genetic drift can also randomly change allele frequencies, especially important over a long time like 2.5 million years.

Diverge by selection into subspecies**
In each area, natural selection favours alleles that give higher fitness there, so different phenotypes increase in frequency. Over time the two gene pools become genetically distinct with some phenotypic differences, forming the two subspecies T. s. solitaria and T. s. cinnamomea, but they can still interbreed so are not yet fully reproductively isolated.

Final answer: Geographical isolation / barrier separated eastern and western populations; no or reduced interbreeding / gene flow between them; different mutations occur in each population; different selection pressures / environmental conditions in east and west; natural selection and / or genetic drift change allele frequencies, leading to allopatric subspeciation.

hints: Recall what a DNA barcode actually compares - the 648 base pair sequence of the cytochrome c oxidase I gene. What would you expect if two birds really belong to the same gene pool?
Think about how to use the size of the difference - a tiny difference between these two forms compared with a much larger difference to other Haematopus species.
walkthrough:
Same barcode means same species**
DNA barcoding sequences the same 648 base pair region of the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase I gene in both birds. If American and black oystercatchers are not separate species, that barcode region will be almost identical in both, even though feather colour looks different.

Judge by size of difference**
You would see only a very small number of base differences between them, typical of variation within a species. Crucially, that difference would be much smaller than the difference between either of them and a truly different species. That pattern indicates they belong to one species.

Final answer: Cytochrome c oxidase I gene / DNA / base sequences of the two forms are (nearly) identical / very similar, with only a small number of base differences / low percentage difference; difference to other species is greater.

hints: Think about the practical problem for a customs officer - many specimens are fragments, eggs, feathers or processed products that cannot be identified by eye. What does a hand-held sequencer allow them to do on the spot?
Once the species is known quickly, think about the actions that follow - checking legal status and then stopping illegal trade.
walkthrough:
Identify quickly and reliably**
A hand-held device lets officers sequence the barcode and match it to the online reference database in minutes, without needing an expert taxonomist. That works even for meat, skin, feathers, eggs or powdered products where morphology is useless.

Enforce protection**
The identification can be checked against the Red List or CITES appendices to see if the specimen is endangered and its trade is restricted or banned. Officers can then confiscate, destroy or relocate the specimens and prosecute smugglers and traders, so illegal trade is stopped and wild populations are protected.

Final answer: Allows rapid / automatic identification of species, even by non-experts, by comparison with reference database / Red List / IUCN list / CITES appendix; then endangered species / products can be confiscated / destroyed and smugglers / traders / poachers prosecuted, preventing trade.
